content: Miliary tuberculosis is a specific form of tuberculosis characterized by widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis throughout the body. The hallmark of this condition is the presence of numerous small lesions, typically 1-5 millimeters in size, which are visible on imaging studies such as chest X-rays. These lesions resemble millet seeds, which is the origin of the term miliary tuberculosis. This form of tuberculosis can affect multiple organs, including the lungs, liver, and spleen, and accounts for approximately 1-3% of all tuberculosis cases. The pathophysiology of tuberculosis begins with the inhalation of airborne droplets containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These droplets are expelled into the air when an infected individual coughs or sneezes. Once inhaled, the bacteria establish small areas of infection in the lungs, known as granulomas, which are localized collections of immune cells attempting to contain the infection. Disseminated tuberculosis, or miliary tuberculosis, occurs in a subset of individuals whose immune systems fail to adequately contain the primary infection. This dissemination can occur within weeks of the initial infection or, in some cases, years later. The risk of developing miliary tuberculosis is significantly higher in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or those taking immunosuppressive medications. Infants and elderly individuals are also at increased risk due to their relatively weaker immune defenses. Patients with miliary tuberculosis often present with non-specific symptoms, including low-grade fever, persistent cough, and generalized lymphadenopathy. In some cases, the disease may manifest with hepatomegaly (enlarged liver) in approximately 40% of cases, splenomegaly (enlarged spleen) in about 15% of cases, and less commonly, pancreatitis in fewer than 5% of cases. Severe cases may involve multi-organ dysfunction, including adrenal insufficiency. Tuberculosis is a preventable disease, even in individuals who have been exposed to an infected person. Secondary prevention strategies include the use of skin testing, such as the tuberculin skin test, to identify latent tuberculosis infection in high-risk populations. These populations include healthcare workers and individuals who have been in close contact with someone diagnosed with tuberculosis. Early detection and treatment of latent tuberculosis can prevent progression to active disease, including miliary tuberculosis.
